To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) pigeons prefer to choose an alternative that provides more immediate access to food and that (b) this preference is stronger when the alternative provides food that is more valuable.

pigeons are not optimal foragers, but they may be optimal in a relative sense.
delay reduction is a more general and useful principle for explaining choice than is the simple maximization of the rate of reinforcement.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

delay reduction's predictions are upheld in a broad range of conditions, but the conditions in which rate maximization is upheld appear limited to those in which the predictions of the two theories are consistent.

the delay-reduction theory is a very powerful and useful theory for explaining the effects of delay on behavior and for explaining choice between alternatives with different delays to reinforcement, and that the theory has been shown to generalize to a variety of different situations.
delay reduction is a useful principle for understanding choice behavior, even in cases in which it may not be the only principle at work.
The main takeaway from our work is that
delay reduction theory can be extended to schedules that better mimic the effort of search.
the delay-reduction hypothesis can be used to predict the effects of foraging on choice, even when the foraging is not directly reinforced by food.
the delay-reduction theory is consistent with foraging behavior, and it is not necessary to invoke the maximization of rate of reinforcement to explain foraging behavior.
